headline: From a 3D Printer in a Suitcase to Dreams of NASA
meta_description: Student Makers brings free STEM education to three continents through student instructors and donated technology, starting with a 3D printer sent to Kenya.
summary_short: A high school student's winter break idea evolved into a global nonprofit teaching STEM to underserved students across the US, Kenya, and India.
body:
When Dilan Mehta packed a 3D printer into his father's suitcase bound for Kenya Relief Academy in Migori, he wasn't launching a nonprofit—he was solving a practical problem. The school served 800 students, including roughly 170 to 190 orphaned children, and had zero STEM infrastructure. What started as remote training sessions three times a week, often interrupted by rain-caused Wi-Fi outages, became something larger: a blueprint for how student teachers could bring advanced technology education to places that needed it most. Today, Jacob, a ninth-grader who learned robotics through the program, leads the academy's robotics team and dreams of becoming a rocket engineer at NASA.

Student Makers itself was founded in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior in California, who created space for students interested in making and technology. The nonprofit now operates across the United States, Kenya, and India, with every instructor drawn from its own student ranks—most still in high school. What makes the model distinctive is its fourth pillar: serve. Dilan added this step after realizing the workshops initially reached only students who already had resources. By embedding service into the framework alongside learning, making, and showcasing, Student Makers ensures knowledge flows toward those with the greatest need.

The expansion happened organically, through family connections and genuine relationships. When Rohan Naegle brought the program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, he was following a lead from his grandfather. More than 25 secondary students have now completed the program there. The recruitment pipeline works the same way everywhere: at each cycle's end, instructors are invited to return and teach. Usually one or two say yes. They already understand the program from inside, making them natural teachers of what matters most—not just technical skills, but the willingness to show up, troubleshoot over spotty internet, and believe in students they've never met in person.
